title: Salesforce Objects, Records, and Fields
objectives: Classify a business requirement as an object, field, record, or value and justify the classification.
Distinguish standard from custom objects using semantic fit rather than label similarity.
Separate metadata changes from business-data changes and choose the appropriate operation boundary.
Diagnose whether an observation concerns structure, presentation, or access before proposing a fix.
diagnostic_question: A company wants to track every equipment inspection, its date, result, inspector, and related customer. Which parts are objects, fields, records, and values—and what evidence would change your answer?
definition: An object defines one category of business information, fields define the facts each instance can hold, and a record is one saved instance. In the official database analogy: object ≈ table, field ≈ column, record ≈ row. ([Salesforce Object Reference](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.object_reference.meta/object_reference/sforce_api_objects_concepts.htm))
why_it_matters: Every report, Flow, Apex query, Lightning component, integration, sharing rule, and deployment assumes a data model. A weak model spreads ambiguity downstream; a precise model gives every actor the same nouns, identities, and state boundaries.

terminology.plain: The organized plan for what the business stores and how those pieces connect.
terminology.precise: The collection of objects, fields, and relationships that structures business data in an org.
terminology.example: A service model with Request, Customer, and Request Line Item objects.
terminology.non_example: A dashboard that summarizes requests; it presents data but is not the storage structure itself.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Database: the underlying storage system; the data model is the human-meaningful structure placed on it.
terminology.boundary: This topic covers objects, fields, and records; relationship behavior is the next topic.

terminology.plain: A named container for one kind of business thing.
terminology.precise: A Salesforce data structure analogous to a database table; its fields define the shape shared by its records.
terminology.example: Account for companies or LAB_Request__c for service requests.
terminology.non_example: Acme Corporation; that is one Account record, not the Account object.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Tab: a navigation surface that can expose an object; a tab is not the object itself.
terminology.boundary: An object defines structure and platform capabilities; it is not a dedicated database server.

terminology.plain: One named fact that every record of an object can hold.
terminology.precise: A typed attribute on an object, analogous to a database table column.
terminology.example: Status__c as a Picklist field on LAB_Request__c.
terminology.non_example: “Approved”; that is a field value inside one record.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Field value: data stored in a field for one record.
terminology.boundary: A field definition is metadata; the value stored for a record is business data.

terminology.plain: One saved instance of the thing described by an object.
terminology.precise: A particular occurrence of an object, analogous to one row in a database table.
terminology.example: Request R-1042 with Status = New and Amount = 1200.
terminology.non_example: The Request object definition shared by all requests.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Record type: metadata that can vary processes, picklist values, and layouts; it is not a record.
terminology.boundary: Records contain business values but remain subject to object, field, and record access controls.

terminology.precise: An object created by Salesforce and included in the platform or licensed product.
terminology.non_example: LAB_Request__c created for a company-specific process.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Custom object: created by a customer, partner package, or implementation.
terminology.boundary: Availability and fields can depend on product, edition, license, and org configuration.

terminology.plain: A business container your organization adds for a need Salesforce did not model for you.
terminology.precise: An org-defined object created through configuration or metadata tooling to store organization-specific information.
terminology.example: LAB_Request__c for a bespoke service intake process.
terminology.non_example: Renaming the Account label; the underlying Account object remains standard.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Custom metadata type: configuration records used by applications, not ordinary transactional business records.
terminology.boundary: Creating a custom object changes metadata; creating one of its records changes business data.

terminology.plain: Information that tells Salesforce how the org is structured, behaves, looks, and grants access.
terminology.precise: Configuration describing schema, processes, presentation, authorization, and general org behavior.
terminology.example: The definition of LAB_Request__c and its Status__c picklist field.
terminology.non_example: A request record whose status value is New.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Business data: the operational records and field values the organization works with.
terminology.boundary: Metadata can still contain sensitive names or text; “not business data” does not mean “never sensitive.”

terminology.plain: The actual customer, transaction, or operational facts saved in records.
terminology.precise: Record and field values that directly correspond to the organization’s business.
terminology.non_example: The fact that Status__c is a picklist with allowed values.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Metadata: the definition and configuration that gives business data its shape.
terminology.boundary: Use data APIs or data tools for records; Metadata API manages definitions rather than ordinary records.

terminology.plain: The stable machine-facing name used by code, queries, and integrations.
terminology.precise: A metadata identifier distinct from the user-facing label; it is the name programmatic tools use to address an object or field.
terminology.non_example: “Service Request,” a label users may see.
terminology.boundary: Treat API-name changes as impact-bearing metadata changes; this lesson does not teach rename behavior.

sixty_second_explanation: Imagine a clean register for service requests. The register template is the object. Its headings—Status, Amount, Requested Date—are fields. Each filled line is a record. “New” and “1200” are values inside one record. Salesforce adds security, automation, APIs, and user interfaces around this structure, so the spreadsheet analogy is useful for shape but not a complete platform model.
deeper_explanation: Start with a stable business noun that can have multiple instances. That is an object candidate.
For each instance, identify atomic facts with meaningful data types. Those are field candidates.
A saved instance supplies values for those fields and receives a record identity.

The definitions are schema metadata; the operational values are business data. Salesforce documents these as different responsibility boundaries. ([Metadata API Guide](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_intro.htm))

Objects can be supplied by Salesforce or created for organization-specific concepts. Reuse a standard object only when its meaning fits; do not force an unrelated process into it merely to avoid a custom object.

mental_model.analogy: A typed register: template → headings → filled rows.
where_it_breaks: A Salesforce object is not only storage; it participates in permissions, automation, APIs, reports, and UI.
A tab is navigation, not the object itself.
Relationships, polymorphism, calculated fields, transactions, and multitenant limits need additional models.

visual_model.title: Definition → instance state transition
visual_model.invariant: Every saved value belongs to a field defined for that object; access and automation can still prevent an actor from observing or changing it.

when_to_use: When a requirement names a business thing and you must classify it as a Salesforce object, field, record, or value before anyone opens Setup.
When deciding whether a repeating inspection belongs on Account fields or on its own custom object with its own records.
When a report is empty and you must separate missing object metadata from missing records or missing field access.
When code or an integration should use an API name on an object or field instead of a user-facing label.
when_not_to_use: Do not treat the object-field-record table analogy as a security, sharing, or automation design.
Do not create a new Salesforce object merely because a Lightning page needs another section.
Do not model a one-off display label as a business object with records.
Do not use this fields-and-records lesson to choose lookup versus master-detail; that is a later relationship topic.
configuration_or_code_location: Setup → Object Manager to inspect or configure objects and fields (UI navigation is release-sensitive; verified 2026-08-07).
App Launcher → an app → object tab or list view to work with records when the object is exposed.
SOQL, REST/SOAP APIs, Apex, Flow, and Lightning data services use object/field API names; those mechanisms are taught later.

mechanics.before: The org has no definition for the new concept/attribute
mechanics.after: The org schema exposes a typed place for values
mechanics.observe: Object Manager or metadata/source describe output
mechanics.failure: Missing permissions, dependency conflicts, invalid metadata, or deployment mismatch.

mechanics.trigger: A role must use the new structure
mechanics.before: Metadata exists but the actor may have no access
mechanics.transition: Assign least-privilege object and field access and expose an appropriate experience
mechanics.after: The intended actor can attempt permitted operations
mechanics.failure: Definition exists but create/read/update is blocked or sensitive fields are overexposed.

mechanics.trigger: A business event creates or changes an instance
mechanics.before: Only the shared schema exists, or an older record state exists
mechanics.transition: Validate and persist field values in a record transaction
mechanics.after: One record has a new identity/state or updated values
mechanics.observe: Record UI, API response, report, audit field, or log
mechanics.failure: Validation, automation, permissions, transaction rollback, or concurrency prevents commit.

worked_example.scenario: A service team needs to track requests independently of Cases in a disposable sandbox. Each request is a record of a custom object with typed fields for status, amount, and date—not a blob of text on Account.
inputs: Each request has Status, Amount, Requested Date, and Sensitive Note.
Requests need independent reporting and lifecycle.

decisions.because: Request is a repeatable concept with its own identity and lifecycle.
decisions.rejected: One long text field on Account; it destroys one-record-per-request reporting grain.

decisions.decision: Create typed fields Status__c, Amount__c, Requested_Date__c, Sensitive_Note__c
decisions.because: Each is one recurring fact per request.
decisions.rejected: Encode all facts in the record name.

decisions.because: It is one occurrence of the Request object.
decisions.rejected: Create a new object for every request.

configuration_or_code: Custom object label: Lab Request; API name: LAB_Request__c
Picklist: Status__c = New, In Review, Approved, Rejected
verification: Object Manager shows the object and field definitions.
A permitted user can create and reopen R-1042.
A list view or report returns R-1042 at the correct grain.
A user without Sensitive_Note__c access cannot read it through the intended surface.
worked_example.self_explanation: Why is Amount__c a field rather than a child object in this bounded scenario? What changed in metadata, and what changed in business data?

hands_on_lab.title: Build and inspect LAB_Request__c in a disposable org
hands_on_lab.environment: Fresh Trailhead Playground, scratch org, or disposable Developer Edition only. Never production.
starting_state_checks: No real customer or personally identifiable information.
You can access Setup and Object Manager.
LAB_Request__c does not already exist, or you have a cleanup plan.
steps: Predict the object, field, record, and value mapping before opening Setup.
From Setup, open Object Manager and create custom object Lab Request with API name LAB_Request__c.
Add Status__c (Picklist), Amount__c (Currency), Requested_Date__c (Date), and Sensitive_Note__c (Long Text Area).
Create a tab only if needed for the lab experience; remember the tab is not the object.
Create synthetic record R-1042 with Status New and Amount 1200.
Reopen it and classify what you see as metadata, record, field, or value.
Delete the synthetic record and remove LAB_ metadata using your cleanup manifest when finished.
guided_completion: Given Request as the object, choose data types for Status and Requested Date.
Explain why R-1042 is not metadata.
hands_on_lab.independent_challenge: Model recurring equipment inspections for customer sites. Decide whether Inspection is an object or Account fields; state cardinality, lifecycle, access, reporting grain, and what evidence would reverse your choice.
evidence: Screenshot or exported metadata showing LAB_Request__c and fields.
Record ID or screenshot for synthetic R-1042.
Written classification with at least one analogy boundary.
stop_recovery_cleanup: Stop if the org contains real customer data.
If a name collision occurs, inspect before changing anything; do not overwrite existing metadata.
Delete synthetic records first, then remove LAB_ metadata only after checking dependencies.
hands_on_lab.limitations: This lab verifies configuration and classification at tiny scale; it does not validate large-data-volume behavior, production security, deployment readiness, or integration contracts.

decision_table.signal: One category with many instances and its own identity/lifecycle
decision_table.not: A repeated set of numbered fields

decision_table.signal: One typed fact shared by every instance
decision_table.why: Keeps the fact on the entity it describes.

decision_table.signal: One real occurrence with actual values
decision_table.why: It is business state, not shared schema.

decision_table.signal: Salesforce-supplied concept fits the business semantics
decision_table.why: Reuses platform/product behavior without parallel truth.

decision_table.signal: Distinct business concept has no suitable standard object
decision_table.why: Makes the domain explicit while accepting governance cost.

limitations: The table/row/column analogy does not explain security, automation, transactions, relationships, or licensing.
Available standard objects and fields depend on products, editions, licenses, features, and org configuration.
UI setup paths can change by release; verify immediately before publication.
Mutable numeric object/field limits are deliberately omitted here; consult the live limits/reference documentation for the target org and release.
security_notes: Object existence does not grant access. Object permission, field-level access, record scope, and execution context are distinct gates.
A page layout or tab is not a security boundary.
Metadata can include sensitive names or descriptions; business data can include personal data. Keep both out of source, labs, screenshots, and prompts unless approved.
Use synthetic LAB_ data and least privilege in disposable environments.
common_mistakes: Calling one Account a standard object instead of a record of the Account object.
Using “record type” as a synonym for record.
Creating a custom object for a single attribute.
Flattening a repeatable child lifecycle into numbered parent fields.
Treating metadata deployment success as proof users can operate the feature.

check: Does the user have object access?
Is a tab created and available in the app?
troubleshooting.do_not_assume: No tab does not prove no object.

troubleshooting.symptom: Object opens but a field is missing
check: Confirm field API name and existence.
Test the relevant API or execution context.
troubleshooting.do_not_assume: A layout change grants field security.
Empty output means data was deleted.

production_notes: Write a data dictionary with business definition, owner, classification, retention, API name, and source of truth.
Review naming, cardinality, ownership, sharing, reporting grain, automation density, integration contracts, archival, and package/deployment impact before creating an object.
Deploy metadata and permissions together; run user-context post-deployment checks.
Keep consequential claims mapped to current official sources and revalidate on every seasonal release.

interview_explanation.thirty_seconds: An object is the business category, fields are typed facts about it, and a record is one saved instance. I start with business meaning and cardinality, reuse a standard object when it fits, and create a custom object only for a distinct concept. I also separate schema metadata from business record data and verify object, field, and record access independently.
interview_explanation.two_minutes: The table/column/row analogy is a good first model: object, field, record. Then I add the platform boundaries it omits. Object and field definitions are metadata; record values are business data. A standard object is supplied by Salesforce, while a custom object models organization-specific information. The choice affects security, reporting, automation, APIs, deployments, storage, and governance. In production I validate semantic fit, cardinality, lifecycle, access, reporting grain, integration ownership, and failure behavior—not just whether Setup lets me create it.

mcqs.prompt: Which mapping matches the official Salesforce data-model analogy?

options.A: Object → row; field → table; record → column
options.B: Object → table; field → column; record → row
options.C: Object → tab; field → page; record → app
options.D: Object → database; field → server; record → tenant

mcqs.rationale: An object structures one category of data like a table, fields define attributes like columns, and each record is one occurrence like a row.

distractor_explanations.C: Tabs, pages, and apps are presentation/navigation concepts, not this storage analogy.
distractor_explanations.D: An object is not a database or tenant boundary.

options.A: A particular occurrence of an object

mcqs.rationale: A record is one saved instance, such as one specific Account.

distractor_explanations.B: A field definition describes one attribute shared across records.
distractor_explanations.D: A deployment moves metadata and is not a business record.

mcqs.prompt: Which statement best distinguishes metadata from business data?

options.A: Metadata is always public; business data is always private
options.B: Metadata describes structure and behavior; business data contains operational record values
options.C: Metadata exists only in code; business data exists only in reports

mcqs.rationale: Object and field definitions are schema metadata, while values inside saved records are business data.

distractor_explanations.A: Both metadata and business data can be sensitive.
distractor_explanations.C: Metadata is also created in Setup, and business data is used beyond reports.
distractor_explanations.D: The official documentation explicitly contrasts them.

mcqs.prompt: A company must track equipment inspections that have no suitable standard object. What is the strongest first modeling choice?

options.A: Create one Inspection custom object with fields for inspection facts
options.B: Put every inspection in a custom label
options.C: Create one field on User for every inspection
options.D: Use a tab with no object

mcqs.rationale: A custom object is intended to store organization-specific categories of business information; fields define each inspection’s facts.

distractor_explanations.B: Custom labels store reusable display text, not transactional records.
distractor_explanations.C: Repeated inspections are instances of their own business concept, not user attributes.
distractor_explanations.D: A tab does not provide a data structure by itself.

mcqs.prompt: For LAB_Request__c, where should a request amount be modeled?

options.A: As a Currency field on the object, with a value on each record
options.B: As a separate Salesforce org per amount

mcqs.rationale: Amount is one typed fact shared by request records, so it belongs in a field definition and each record stores its own value.

distractor_explanations.B: Org boundaries are not data values.
distractor_explanations.C: The label names the object for people.
distractor_explanations.D: A profile contributes permissions, not transactional amount storage.

mcqs.prompt: A developer needs the stable identifier used by code while admins want friendly wording for users. Which pairing is correct?

options.A: Use the label for code and the API name only in page layouts
options.B: Use the API name for programmatic references and the label for display
options.C: Use the record ID as the object label
options.D: Use the tab style as the API name

mcqs.rationale: The machine-facing API name and human-facing label serve different audiences.

distractor_explanations.A: Labels can change for display and should not replace programmatic identifiers.
distractor_explanations.C: A record ID identifies one record, not an object label.
distractor_explanations.D: Tab style controls presentation, not schema identity.

mcqs.prompt: A migration script needs to create Account records. Which layer should it operate on?

options.A: Business data through an appropriate data API or data tool
options.B: Only Metadata API because Account is an object

mcqs.rationale: Creating Accounts creates business records. Salesforce documentation distinguishes record operations from metadata operations.

distractor_explanations.B: Metadata API manages definitions and configuration, not ordinary Account record CRUD.
distractor_explanations.D: Tab icons are unrelated presentation metadata.

mcqs.prompt: Users can open Account but cannot see one sensitive field. What does this symptom show?

options.A: Object access alone does not prove field access
options.B: The Account object is necessarily missing
options.D: The field must be a tab

mcqs.rationale: Object, field, and record access are distinct gates. Being able to reach an object does not guarantee visibility of every field.

distractor_explanations.B: The object exists because users can open Account.
distractor_explanations.C: Existing Account pages disprove universal deletion.
distractor_explanations.D: A field and a tab are different concepts.

mcqs.prompt: An admin adds Status__c to LAB_Request__c, then creates request R-1042 with Status = New. Which is metadata and which is data?

options.C: Status__c definition is metadata; R-1042 and New are business data
options.D: R-1042 is metadata; Status__c is data

mcqs.rationale: The field definition gives records their structure; the saved record and field value are operational data.

distractor_explanations.A: The request instance is not configuration.
distractor_explanations.B: The field definition is schema metadata.

mcqs.prompt: A report has no rows for a user, but an admin confirms records exist. What should be investigated before redesigning the object?

options.A: Access, filters, and the user’s data scope
options.B: Whether columns should be renamed records
options.C: Whether a tab can replace all permissions
options.D: Whether Salesforce needs a dedicated server for the object

mcqs.rationale: Missing output can result from filters or access. Existence of an object and records does not guarantee every user or report can return them.

distractor_explanations.B: Renaming concepts does not diagnose missing data.
distractor_explanations.C: A tab cannot replace access controls.
distractor_explanations.D: Salesforce objects are tenant data structures, not dedicated servers.

mcqs.prompt: When should an existing standard object be preferred over a new custom object?

options.A: Whenever its business meaning and behavior fit the requirement without semantic distortion
options.B: Whenever the custom object name would be shorter
options.C: Only when no fields are needed
options.D: Never; custom objects are always safer

mcqs.rationale: Start with the business concept and reuse a standard object when its meaning fits. Create a custom object for organization-specific concepts that do not fit.

distractor_explanations.B: Name length is not a modeling criterion.
distractor_explanations.C: Standard objects have fields and support extension.
distractor_explanations.D: Custom is not automatically safer or better.

mcqs.prompt: Which statement correctly compares a field and a record?

options.A: A field defines one attribute; a record supplies values for the object’s fields
options.B: A field contains many orgs; a record defines a permission set
options.C: A field is always custom; a record is always standard
options.D: They are interchangeable names for a row

mcqs.rationale: The field is part of the shared schema; the record is one instance containing values that conform to that schema.

distractor_explanations.C: Both standard and custom objects can have fields; records are instances, not standard/custom schema categories.
distractor_explanations.D: Only the record maps to a row in the analogy.

interview_questions.question: Explain objects, fields, and records to a nontechnical stakeholder.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: An object is the category of thing we track, a field is one fact about it, and a record is one actual instance.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I start from the business noun, such as Service Request. Salesforce represents that category with an object. Amount, status, and requested date become typed fields. Every submitted request becomes a record whose values follow that shared structure. The table/column/row analogy is useful for structure, but it does not explain permissions, automation, or user interface behavior.
interview_questions.example: LAB_Request__c has Status__c and Amount__c; R-1042 is one record.
tradeoffs: The analogy is bounded; Salesforce objects also participate in security, automation, APIs, and UI.
weak_answer_warnings: Uses record type as a synonym for record.

interview_questions.question: Differentiate standard and custom objects.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Standard objects are supplied by Salesforce; custom objects are added for organization-specific concepts. I choose by semantic fit, not by habit.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Account and Contact are common standard objects. If the required business concept fits one of them, I extend rather than duplicate. If the concept is independently meaningful and no standard object fits, I define a custom object. I still check product licensing, ownership, security, reporting, relationships, integrations, and lifecycle before committing.
interview_questions.example: Use Account for a customer company; use LAB_Request__c for a bespoke service intake entity.
tradeoffs: A custom object adds metadata and governance cost. A standard object can carry product behaviors that must fit the requirement.
follow_ups: What if the standard object almost fits?
How would you migrate from a poor choice?

interview_questions.question: A business asks for ten new fields on Account to track inspections. What do you ask before building?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I ask whether inspection is a repeatable business entity with its own lifecycle, ownership, reporting, and relationships. If yes, it likely deserves an Inspection object rather than ten flattened Account fields.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I clarify cardinality: can one account have many inspections? I ask which actors create and approve them, which facts repeat, whether history matters, how access differs, and what reports or integrations need. The state transition matters: an inspection moves through statuses; an Account usually persists across many inspections. That evidence drives object versus field choice.
interview_questions.example: If an Account has quarterly inspections, Inspection__c records related to Account preserve one row per event.
tradeoffs: Another object increases relationship, sharing, reporting, and automation complexity; a field can be correct for a true one-value attribute.
follow_ups: How would you prevent duplicate inspections?
weak_answer_warnings: Models a repeatable process as a single text blob.

interview_questions.question: Users can see Account records but not Revenue__c. Diagnose without guessing.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I separate object, field, and record gates. Record visibility proves only part of access; I inspect field-level access and the presentation/API path.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I reproduce as the affected user, confirm the exact object and field API name, and distinguish “not visible on page” from “not readable at all.” Then I inspect field-level security, permission sets/groups, page or component visibility, and the execution context of any code or integration. I use evidence from UI/API behavior rather than assuming the field is missing.
interview_questions.example: The field may exist and be readable to admins but omitted or denied for one permission set group.
tradeoffs: A layout fix does not grant field permission; changing FLS can expose data across more surfaces than intended.
follow_ups: What if Apex returns the field?
What if only one record is affected?

interview_questions.question: A report shows zero requests although admins see hundreds. What is your investigation path?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: First verify report type and filters, then the running user’s object, field, and record scope. I do not redesign the schema until I can locate the failing gate.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I capture the user, report URL, expected record IDs, filter values, date/time zone, report type, and folder context. I compare a known record against report criteria, then inspect whether the user can query/open it and read fields used by filters. This moves from observation to falsifiable hypotheses.
interview_questions.example: R-1042 exists, but its owner is outside the user’s record scope or Status__c is unavailable to the reporting path.
tradeoffs: Changing filters can leak data; broadening sharing to fix one report may violate least privilege.
follow_ups: How would you prove it is record access?

interview_questions.question: A deployment added an object but production users cannot create records. What layers do you check?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I verify the metadata arrived, then permissions, field requirements, layouts or actions, validation/automation failures, and licensing.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: A successful metadata deployment only proves definitions were accepted. I check the object and fields in Object Manager or describe output, assigned permissions, required fields, record types, create action exposure, validation rules, Flows/Apex errors, and user license constraints. I reproduce with a minimal record and retain the exact error.
interview_questions.example: The object exists, but the permission set was not assigned or a required field is absent from the create experience.
tradeoffs: Granting Modify All is not a diagnostic. Disabling automation can hide the actual defect.
weak_answer_warnings: Treats deploy success as user readiness.
Asks users to retry without reading the error.

interview_questions.question: Defend using a custom object instead of adding fields to Case.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I use a custom object when the concept has its own identity, lifecycle, cardinality, access, and integration contract; I extend Case when it is truly a case attribute or supported case process.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I compare semantic fit, one-to-many behavior, ownership/sharing, required state transitions, reporting grain, automation density, API consumers, archival, and product features. A custom object isolates a distinct aggregate but adds relationships and governance. Extending Case reuses Service features but can overload its meaning.
interview_questions.example: A regulated inspection with multiple readings and approvals may be independent from the support Case that initiated it.
tradeoffs: Custom objects add metadata, security, storage, reporting, and deployment work; Case may provide valuable service capabilities.
follow_ups: What are your decisive nonfunctional requirements?

interview_questions.question: The stakeholder calls a record type “a kind of record.” How do you correct the model tactfully?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I acknowledge the wording, then separate an individual record from Record Type metadata that can vary business process, picklists, and presentation for records on the same object.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I use two examples on one object: R-1042 and R-1043 are records. “Warranty Request” and “Billing Request” can be record types applied to those records. The record type classifies/configures behavior; it is not the saved business instance. Then I ask what difference the stakeholder actually needs—different data, lifecycle, access, or merely presentation.
interview_questions.example: Two Case records can have different record types while remaining records of the Case object.
tradeoffs: Record types add maintenance and do not create a new security boundary or object.
follow_ups: When would separate objects be better?
Does record type grant record access?
weak_answer_warnings: Claims record types are separate tables.

flashcards.back: A named Salesforce structure for one category of business information; analogous to a table.
A typed attribute on an object; analogous to a column.
One saved occurrence of an object; analogous to a row.
An object Salesforce creates and supplies.
An org-defined object for organization-specific information.

flashcards.front: Should “Acme Corporation” be an object or record? Why?
flashcards.back: A record: it is one occurrence of the Account business concept.

flashcards.front: Should “inspection date” be an object, field, or record?
flashcards.back: Usually a Date field on an Inspection object; it is one fact per inspection.
When its business meaning and supported behavior fit without semantic distortion.
When a stable, independently useful business concept has multiple instances and no suitable standard object.

flashcards.front: What should code use: label or API name?
flashcards.back: The API name; labels are human-facing display text.

flashcards.front: Does object access guarantee field visibility?
flashcards.back: No. Object, field, and record access are distinct gates.
Yes. Names, descriptions, reports, or configuration text can contain sensitive information.

flashcards.front: Does the object/field/record analogy explain permissions or automation?
flashcards.back: No. It explains structure only; security, behavior, and transaction mechanics require separate models.

flashcards.front: You add Status__c, then save Status = New. Classify both.
flashcards.back: Status__c definition is metadata; New on a saved record is business data.

flashcards.front: A report is empty although records exist. First hypothesis categories?
flashcards.back: Filters, report type/shape, and user access/data scope—not immediately a missing object.

review_schedule.prompt: From memory, draw object → fields → one record → values for LAB_Request__c. Mark metadata versus business data.
Classify five new examples: Account, Acme, Industry, Manufacturing, and Account tab. Explain one confusable neighbor.
Decide whether recurring inspections belong in Account fields or an Inspection object; name the variables that control the decision.
Diagnose: object visible, one field missing, report empty. Separate structure, presentation, and access hypotheses.
Teach the model without saying object, field, or record; then answer a skeptical probe about where the table analogy breaks.

mermaid.structure:
flowchart TD
  Obj[Object: category of thing] --> Fld[Fields: typed facts]
  Fld --> Rec[Record: one saved instance]
  Rec --> Val[Values in those fields]
  Obj --> Std[Standard object supplied by Salesforce]
  Obj --> Cust[Custom object for org-specific concepts]
  Fld --> Meta[Field definition is metadata]
  Rec --> Data[Record values are business data]
mermaid.sequence:
sequenceDiagram
  participant Admin
  participant OM as Object Manager
  participant User
  Admin->>OM: Define object and fields metadata
  User->>OM: Create a record with values
  User->>User: Report or UI shows that record if access allows

claims.claim: Salesforce objects and fields are analogous to database tables and columns; a record is analogous to a row.
claims.validation: Both official pages render the same mapping.

claims.claim: Standard objects are supplied by Salesforce; custom objects are created to store organization-specific information.
claims.validation: Cross-checked in Developer and Trailhead pages.

claims.claim: Salesforce metadata describes schema, process, presentation, authorization, and org configuration, while business data includes operational records and values.
Metadata API manages customization definitions and not ordinary business record CRUD.
claims.validation: Verified exact rendered passage and linked data-API contrast.

claims.claim: Application access to objects and data depends on org definitions/configuration, user permissions, access settings, sharing, and object-specific factors.
claims.scope: API access orientation, not a complete security algorithm

claims.claim: Object relationships are relationship fields that connect objects; detailed relationship behavior is a separate topic.
